title: Getting People Comfortable With a Decision They Think Is Wrong
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article tackles a common leadership blind spot: telling people to simply accept a decision they dislike instead of helping them process it. The author suggests leaders take partial ownership of the discomfort a decision causes, even when they weren't the direct cause of it, by asking a disappointed colleague what would help them feel more comfortable with the outcome. The piece frames this as an act of empathy that changes how the decision and the leader are perceived, even when nothing about the decision itself can change. It closes by suggesting that the willingness to help matters more than any actual remedy offered.
points: Telling people to grow up and accept a decision tends to harden resistance rather than reduce it
Good leaders take some ownership of a team member's discomfort even if they didn't cause it
Ask directly: What can I do to get you more comfortable with the decision?
The willingness to help, more than any concrete fix, is what eases hard feelings
quotes: Getting comfortable with an unpopular or detrimental decision can be extremely difficult for people.
By taking responsibility for their discomfort, good leaders flip the script and promote acceptance of the decision.
The critical move is to engage the disappointed colleague with a simple question: What can I do to get you more comfortable with the decision?
Sometimes it is not the help but the desire to help that soothes hard feelings.
Placing the burden of their discomfort partially on your shoulders as a leader will likely change how they view both you and the decision.
